# Redirect to a URL from HTTP request data (Python)

`qualor:python/open-redirect` · Issue · Severity: Medium · [CWE-601](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/601.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A01:2025 Broken Access Control](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A01_2025-Broken_Access_Control/), [A01:2021 Broken Access Control](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A01_2021-Broken_Access_Control/)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
Redirects whose target comes from the HTTP request: Flask's and Werkzeug's `redirect()`, Django's
`redirect()`, `HttpResponseRedirect` and `HttpResponsePermanentRedirect`, and FastAPI's or
Starlette's `RedirectResponse`, when request data decides the whole target or its scheme and host.
URLs the application builds for its own views (`url_for()`, `reverse()`) and request data after a
fixed path or origin are not reported.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
A link such as `https://shop.example/login?next=https://evil.example` looks like a link to your
site, but after signing in the user lands on another one. Attackers use this for convincing
phishing pages and to carry tokens from a sign-in flow to a host they control.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** the `next` parameter is the whole redirect target.

```python
from flask import Flask, redirect, request

app = Flask(__name__)


@app.route("/after-login")
def after_login():
    return redirect(request.args.get("next", "/"))
```

**Compliant:** the parameter only picks one of a few fixed targets.

```python
from flask import Flask, redirect, request

app = Flask(__name__)

TARGETS = {"orders": "/orders", "settings": "/settings"}


@app.route("/after-login")
def after_login():
    return redirect(TARGETS.get(request.args.get("next"), "/"))
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Redirect to a URL the application builds for its own views: `url_for()` in Flask, `reverse()`
  in Django.
- Keep the scheme and host fixed and put request data after a path: `"/items/" + item_id`, or
  `SITE + "/items/" + item_id`.
- Or pick the target from an allow-list (a module-level dict of constants).
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- Flask
- Werkzeug
- Django
- django-hosts
- FastAPI
- Starlette

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- A fixed origin is recognised as a literal, an upper-case module constant holding a literal URL,
  or a Django setting, at the start of the URL text. `%`-formatting with a constant origin
  (`"%s/items/%s" % (SITE, id)`) and long chains of concatenation are not recognised, so such code
  is reported.
- A check of the parsed host (`urlparse(x).netloc`) or Django's
  `url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme()` is not recognised.
- A slice is followed when it slices request data in place (`request.args["next"][:200]`),
  a variable assigned request data, or a view parameter; a slice of a value built from request
  data (`(request.args["q"] + "x")[:50]`), or of a variable assigned again after the request value
  (`q = q.strip()`, also `q = q + request.args["b"]` or a fallback `q = request.form["q"]`), is
  missed.
- The current request's own path counts as a path on this site, although a path that starts with
  `//` names another host.
- Values returned by a database query or another call are taken for stored data, unless the call
  receives request data whole; a request value passed to such a call through a variable is missed.
- An allow-list is recognised only as a lookup in a module-level dict of literals assigned to an
  upper-case name that is never changed, or as a ternary of constants.
- Request sources are recognised by their shape: a Flask `<int:n>` route parameter and a numeric
  Django URL argument still count as request data, and a function whose first parameter is named
  `request` in a Django module is taken for a view.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

lines marked `ruleid:` must be reported and lines marked `ok:` must not. The known limits are
